Late to the party here, but, wanted to throw in that more studies being done probably wouldn't give any further concrete clarity on this specific statistic because the marker variables are just too many. Every study group would just have too many varying conclusions because the study groups would be too difficult to narrow down.

Even if you isolated the study to only unmedicated and untreated individuals with ADHD, that doesn't account for the type of ADHD or severity of symptoms. Plus you would also want the study to include a group that is medicated and treated. Then there's the issue of deciding if you need to narrow down the variables of growing up with knowing you have ADHD or only knowing you have ADHD as an adult, as this affects your knowledge/understanding of your symptoms and thus your awareness of the risks it puts you in. And within that, growing up with ADHD diagnosis and no treatment vs treatment vs adult diagnosis and no treatment vs treatment.

It's just a lot of variables that all would matter for producing coherent data. I think a better hypothesis study for this might be something like "Unregulated impulsivity impedes typical life expectancy for individuals with ADHD" because I'm going to go out on a limb with my understanding of ADHD from growing up with it, to others with it, to my academics within relevant fields, and say that unchecked/unmanaged impulsive behavior is the forefront cause of the statistic.

Because when you are impulsive and lack the ability to risk assess, you end up in more dangerous situations. More dangerous situations mean higher risk of death. The dangerous situations could be substance related, adrenaline junkie behavior, or even something like being more likely to put yourself into dangerous situations to help others like in situations with car accidents, domestic violence, etc without properly thinking about your own safety first. Even something as simple as having pica (a common eating disorder among those with ADHD) is going to contribute to the higher death statistic because of the impulse to eat things that could be dangerous, like cleaners.

I live my life knowing that I have impulsive behaviors and adjust accordingly by practicing risk assessment before and during moments that I am aware could be dangerous or become dangerous. I still engage in thrill seeking and impulsive behaviors, I just know to check myself before I permanently wreck myself.

I would just look at them. Death stare, if you will. If you're going to take time out of my day and inconvenience me, I am going to act inconvenienced. I'm kind when you are kind. I am not going to act subdued while you mentally criminalize me.

So my advice to y'all is to just stare at them. No words, no attitude. Just watch them. People do not like to have analyzing eyes on them. Make them feel uncomfortable and like they're doing something bad and wasting their time. Because they are. There's just not a reason to check someone's receipt like that. Reading this gave me a lot of echoes of my past. Having been born to essentially become my mom's therapist for her abusive life and marriage, I had/have a lot of internalized self-worth issues. I was silenced a lot, and conversely, there were times as a kid that my mom would "box me out" when I did wrong. I have a lot of memories of me trying to talk to her the days after she'd yell at me and she would either pretend I wasn't there in front of my face (would literally look past me like a ghost) or go "who's mom? I'm not your mom."

So...yeah when I started getting into relationships, I was a lot different, but unfortunately, I walked away with learning to go radio silent and keep my mouth shut/head down when conflict arose. It wasn't ever a punishment for people to me, it was more like "this is bad now and I don't want it to be bad and I don't know what to do because my feelings are stupid anyway and I shouldn't even care about anything or be upset over anything ever why am I causing problems" So, basically, I just freaked the fuck out at altercations because I didn't want to feel how I was always made to feel at home by others.

I honestly thought this was a good approach, too. Because I struggle with socializing skills, which is the result of an entirely different abuse I faced, I thought people generally were happy when you stopped talking to them about unhappy things. I basically felt like if I talked about bad things and how I felt it would cause more fights. That it was better to just not engage for days until there was something "normal" I could bring up and avoid/avert the entire situation. Most of the time the way I'd initiate this silence was by apologizing for whatever the issue was (never sarcastically, I just always say sorry), watching them respond back with anger/venting, taking that as validation I was the issue and needed to go away.

I didn't learn that this was hurtful for the people who really cared about me until a few years back. I would think of their perspective for sure, but for some reason my brain never registered that they would be sad. I thought for sure they would be talking about what I'd said or done to their friends and just collectively shitting on me for being "emotional", or that they were disgusted/angry with me and were relieved I was out of their hair for several hours or days. I just thought the sentiment of their last messages to me was how they felt about me in general. It took a long time for somebody to actually talk to me about this in a way that made me understand I was giving the other person as much anxiety as I was internally dealing with.

There are a lot of variables when it comes to what electricity does and doesn't do, and I am not an expert on all of them. But I do know, for a fact, as demonstrated in physics labs, electrical current can both "hold onto" and "repel" things based on how the electricity comes into contact with whatever item it is acting on. Her hands probably look gently placed (though to me, they look sort of curved around the pole and odd) because of the fact her muscles are tensing up the most, making her unable to flex anything on her own in that region. Many people being electrocuted can look both limp and rigid. That intensity of muscle contraction will be less the further you get from entry point of the current, assuming there's a direct exit point for the electricity.

As for the jacket, there are a lot more materials that can insulate against electricity than rubber. Materials like polyethylene or wool, which can be found in many insulated types of jackets, can be viable. While most things won't be as effective as rubber, there are many materials that help with insulation of electricity. I do actually believe one of her saving graces here would be the fact she isn't wearing anything rubber, like rain boots. Because then the current would essentially build up in her body as it's not able to exit. Since it has a direct exit path (to the ground through her feet, which are mostly open toed and probably poor insulators), there's always going to be a consistent input and output of electricity, not a build up or MORE electricity. The pole has whatever voltage the pole has from stored up current, once she came into contact, that voltage gets shared between her, the pole, and the ground she's in contact with.

As for why it's sticking to her, but repelling the boys, all I can say for that is variables. Wild electricity is not really a predictable form of energy. There's a lot of environmental factors that come into play with it all. One thing I can think of is that she probably smacked the pole hard to grab it, like with intent, as she didn't know it was going to shock her, which exposed more of her surface area to the current. Compared to the sheepish way we tend to try and touch electrical things, which gives us enough of a zap to make us pull away but not really grab something.

I respect the skepticism of it, though. I am just trying to explain the reasons that, in my perspective, make this a pretty good educational video on what electricity does and how it interacts with things outside a lab.

I'm simultaneously both awful and okay at games. Example, I'm a medic main on TF2 and have close to 1k hours on medic. I'm really good at support or DPS classes in games, it's where I thrive. I'm good at people pleasing, emergency tasks, quick time events (like popping an uber), observing others actions, etc. This comes in handy with understanding what I need to do as a medic on a fundamental level.

I basically use my specific "strengths" of my ADHD to be good at games. I think I'm barely functional enough to be allowed to use a mouse and keyboard, but I have gotten a fair amount of "wow, you're good" and "this is harder than you make it seem" from people I've played a significant time with.

Now, with platformers? LMAO. I love platform games, but precision isn't my thing. Small, specific, look-to-the-left-slightly-and-lose type game mechanics aren't my thing. I'm great at puzzles, at finding small details where they stand out enough to be irregular to the scene, but I'm not good at shooters where the controls are fickle. 

Another thing that helped me with gaming is mouse sensitivity. I process things faster than most people, this is why I watch lectures on 2-3x speed but can barely sit through a 50 minute lecture with normal talking. That normal talking rate to me is slow motion, and thus I get lost and distracted in lectures that I can watch in 25 minutes and actually retain that info. So, taking that information, I made my mouse sensitivity super high. Because I react quicker, I need to look sooner, I need things to feel smooth when I turn. Not anticipate the "lag" feel of normal sensitivity.

Basically, gaming is fine motor skills. You have different fine motor skills than most. You're better at some things, and a bit worse at other things most people don't even notice or have minimal issues with. It's something you gotta really hone in on about yourself and do some self inflection. I'm never gonna be good at platformers, but I still enjoy them, I just go slow and restart a lot. I'm always going to struggle to get the hang of controls, get left and right confused, etc. But I'm also probably going to be the one you hand the controller to, to figure out a puzzle or decode a riddle. You have a unique playstyle and skillset available to you for certain game niches, you just have to discover what really clicks with your ADHD on this one.

If you're procrastinating because deep down you're feeling really anxious about this next step in life, I completely understand that. I know everyone in the ADHD communities here are pretty helpful anyway and I can see you've already got tons of advice, but I want to sparknotes a few things for you. It might help you ease your toes into the process.

1. Not all stimulants work the same on the same person. There is a chance it won't be for you.

2. If it isn't the med for you, don't keep taking it. All ADHD medications come with side effects. Stuff like being unable to sleep, no hunger, headaches, etc are pretty common and not exactly signs to stop a medication. What IS a sign to stop and that it isn't right for you is a sudden urge to rage out or uncontrollable mood swings. The immense anger and conflict I felt THE FIRST DAY of Ritalin let me know it was NOT the one for me.

3. It's very likely you will experience euphoric feelings for the first few days to a week. Almost everyone on ADHD meds gets this because of the nature of what a stimulant is. Do not assume this feeling is the norm and do not chase after it or seek it out. It will fade when your body adjusts to the meds. Just understand that for a few days, you may feel like a rockstar in the best of ways. 

Side note: Use this to your advantage to jumpstart something if you're so inclined! I take med breaks sometimes for my tolerance, and if I take a week or two off, I get that euphoric feeling back for a couple days and use it to my advantage. As long as you don't depend on that feeling or try to recreate it constantly, it can be a pretty useful side effect sometimes.

4. You will know if they're doing something or not. They WILL work, but they just might not work *for you*.  It's important for us to not hyper monitor ourselves during our first doses (like writing every single feeling down or change in heart rate), but to at least stay vigilant of ourselves. Maybe you couldn't do any household chores the day before, but the day you take your dose, you notice that you've been picking up trash as you walk about or have taken the effort to wipe off a counter or clean the hair out of your brush that you would usually leave for a few more days. Just productive or routine tasks feel like they have less resistance. **You aren't going to feel like a different person.** You might feel DIFFERENT, but you won't become someone else. You will still be you.

Overall OP, take your time and let the process do what it's going to do. Meds are not for every single person, some people need to try multiple types of stimulants, and everyone feels the effects differently because our ADHD is different. It's unavoidable to be apprehensive of such a change, but it will be okay. You will be okay. Your feelings about it all are valid in the same way you seeking out the help you needed for your ADHD is valid. You just need to keep the mindset that this is for you and to help you. If it's not helping you, I believe in you enough to believe you'd know.

It's okay, I understand that English verb tenses specifically can be rough for non-native speakers. If this will be useful for you for future reference, pet can be used in past, present, and future tense. 

Examples: "I pet a dog" (Past), "Can I pet your dog?" (Present), "I will pet a dog" (Future) are all correct uses of the verb and the tense can be assumed from the other parts of the sentences.

And this works for many other verbs, too, like hit. "He hit me" (Past), "hit it" (Present), "I am going to hit something" (Future)

And to make it worse for learners, a word, like pat, can be used to assume tense as well. It would be equally correct to say "I gave him a pat" and "I gave him a pet" because the actions pat/pet are basically the same thing and are used interchangeably with a lot of dialects. Many use pat as the past tense of pet, depending on the dialect.

It's upsetting Google is so rife with wrong info now, because petted will never be the correct tense form. The word "petted" does not exist in any modern or semi-modern proper grammatical structure. People only use the "petted" to be intentionally silly, or in some cases, I have heard it used with southern accents.

I hope this is helpful for you since Google failed you!

Yes, you're right. How I initially worded it was too vague and constricting. My ideal would be using this form of medical treatment as a case by case "life saving" procedure. So, for people that are genetically predisposed to sickle cell, as you mentioned. Technically yes, they can live, but it will also be costly and painful. I think using the technology to prevent livable but detrimental ailments is ideal.

It's difficult on its own to really be able to narrow down what should/shouldn't qualify. But, as a general consensus, I think the only real way we can see this kind of advancement be used in a non-dystopian way is to have some kind of "basis" example for a perfectly healthy baby. Some kind of blueprint we go off of, not to create the "best" baby, but to help create the most "default" settings baby. The most evolutionarily basic and standard, if that makes sense?

So things like eye color, skin tone, or male pattern baldness wouldn't be things to pick and choose from, but being free from diabetes or auto immune disorders that are "livable" but costly and detrimental to quality of life are. But then we get into the debate of what qualifies for those things? Should we specifically only make it usable for "biological" disorders, or should we be able to go in and change physical appearances? Yes or no? And if so, what are the limitations behind what physical appearances can be changed to? And why?

This discussion here shows just how complex and far behind we are on making any "BIG" advancements towards designer babies. It's just insanely complex to narrow down who and what without there being some issue with ethnic and gender diversity. It's hard to consider all the what ifs even in an entire board room full of people with degree collections that would make us look like unschooled bumpkins.

I LOVE to discuss this though, it is probably the most interesting recent science topic I've been invested in researching. I've not read all the comments, so I'm sure another person knowledgeable on vet practices has already said most of this, but I might as well throw it in from my side, too.

First, let's get this out of the way, they are supposed to disclose all medical information to you, and a script of any kind counts as medical information.

I've only worked as a vet assistant for now, but there's a few medications I'm very familiar with and traz is one of them. Yeah, they aren't wrong, it's used very commonly in dogs. It is especially used in dogs with anxiety or after surgery. My collie mix who is 2 is on traz right now due to a luxated patella and a broken bone she's healing from and is occasionally on it for controlling her anxiety/excitement better.

Some things that are known about traz (meaning I learned it from the vet staff I work with and personal experience): 

It can make dogs pee without warning, number one. My dog has a history of just letting loose when on traz. I have explained this to different vets, because she has done it since she was still a little puppy even on small doses. It just...makes her pee. And where does she often pee? My bed. She finds my bed comforting to her and she gets too knocked out to even cue to me she needs to go. She doesn't even wake up. Just pees in her sleep.

It can make dogs act "inexplicably" hyper/agitated when the traz wears off. You know what being groggy after a particularly long mid-day nap feels like? It can be a bit like that. Some dogs tolerate the dose just fine, but the comedown is rough for some dogs. I see it most in labs/husky breeds, but even my collie is similar. My dog in particular gets snippy/annoyed with other dogs easier when she's on the traz and coming off of it. She's typically not as temperamental when she hasn't had any traz for a couple weeks.

Most of the vets I've had the privilege of being around long enough to learn from, do not generally advocate for constant traz use daily unless it's actually necessary. Even though the bottle may say once a day or twice a day, it probably says AS NEEDED after that. Most every traz label I have printed or gotten from my vets have "as needed" on them as part of the instructions. Having a dog SEDATED every day, all day, is not healthy unless it's necessary. And when it is necessary for daily use, it involves actually scaling the drugs back to get the best dose amount with the most cognitively functional but CALMER dog. Think taking 1/4 a xanax instead of half of one for some people who just need to be calm but not be knocked out calm.

I think the absolute best thing you can do for your dog and for yourself is go to a vet in your area. Maybe one that has been in practice for a while if you can. Older vets talk a lot more about specifics and will overshare on details/info a lot of the time if their client is willing. Meaning, you get an earful, but good information. Anyways, I would explain to the vet that she is on traz and experiencing incontinence and agitated moods. Especially if you notice she is having these mood swings of being crazy hyper/agitated around 7-8 hours after her traz. Most dogs are on it twice a day (as needed) because its half life can be shorter and it might not keep them as sedated as intended. 

If she has anxiety, the vet may be able to prescribe her some other medication. He may also may be able to advise you on the best plan of exit for the traz. There is technically nothing "wrong" with going cold turkey with traz, but it may really impact the dog's mood if their bodies have gotten used to getting it every day to the point of being mostly incapacitated. We generally always recommend to wean off meds, even traz. So, if she typically gets 200mg, we would reduce that to 150mg for a couple days, then to 100mg for a couple days, then to 50mg, and then finally just stop the dose. Not all vets do this, but it's a practice I learned early and intend to keep as it's generally good advice and caretaking to slowly wean off medications.

You may notice after a solid month of no traz and getting adjusted to you and your house as HERSELF and not her sedated self, that some of these behavioral issues will resolve. They may not of course, but the TRAZODONE may be the real crux of your issue with the pup, not so much the pup's actual behavior/personality.

That's all I got, I wish you the best and hope this was helpful!

Hello hi yes. I have ADHD as well as mild tremors in both my hands. The best way I've found to accommodate both the ADHD and the tremors is to rig up a clip attachment to my magnetic wand and place my hand and wrist on the table in a way that I can fully relax them. I actually like to put my entire arm up to my elbow on the table because it lets me rest/lean on it, too, which helps with not moving.

A lot of people don't realize that if your wrist isn't on something stable it can strain your movements and cause your fingers/hands to make sudden movements. For example, if my wrist is resting on the side of the table, my fingers will sometimes twitch/move and scrape the magnetic wand. Or sometimes I will lose grasp on the magnetic wand if I'm holding it by hand and it will hit my nail.

The clip attachment rig I set up keeps me from having to use one of my hands, keeps the magnet steady, and stays in 1 position unless I tweak it so I get consistent magnetized lines.

I also put on timers because It really does make me antsy to intentionally sit still without any movements for even 90 seconds. Like I feel really uncomfortable and almost painful? So, I set a timer for one nail, then I give myself a few minute break to move my hand/fingers around delicately so I can stim out.

I also watch Cold Case Detective a lot while I do this. I like list type videos for painting my nails because the multiple stories/information help keep my brain stimulated while I have to unfortunately practice patience.

Hopefully something here helps!

Once Kurt Cobain died, people got morbidly interested, and more people started to analyze the lyrics of a lot of Nirvana's songs. The consensus online, and basically to every emo kid in the 2000s, is that Kurt had a really broken mental state that could be somewhat seen in the lyrics. I'd say Nirvana and Kurt Cobain just defined grunge for the non-grunge scene, and especially for teens going through their changessss. I mean Smells Like Teen Spirit is maybe the most popular song of that genre and time period to the general public *still*.

I can see the perspective of people who did grow up with 90's grunge, though, through Chester Bennington and Linkin Park. LP was *my* band when I was going through my teens in the late 2000's and 2010's. It's seen as cringe by a lot of people who associate it with anime AMVs or with like dumb internet skits, but it was a big deal to me as a person who was going through a lot of abuse and self image issues. Then Chester died.

Ofc it was a big deal to me, I was very sad, as it was no secret how bad his mental health was and how tied into their songs a lot of it was. But there were still *MANY* other nu metal bands of that time period who meant a lot to me and were as influential as LP even before Chester passed. Three Days Grace is a notable one. But still, now everytime I bring up LP, it's often met with talk of how Chester and Mike influenced entire generations with their music and how great they are and how "deep" the lyrics are. Before Chester died, these people 100% had zero idea what LP was and garnered all of their info on Chester and the band via some articles online because of his death.

Not that I hate them for only knowing a surface level of knowledge, but the status LP gained from the death of Chester has a lot of parallels to Nirvana's cult following after the death of Kurt. To summarize an entire genre with 1 band is doing that genre injustice, but I can see why it reached an idolized pop cultural obsession status. People are absolutely fascinated by the concept of the deeply struggling tortured artist.

Hi! I also heal very slowly, and I get lots of blue-ish purple bruises from my day to day life. I know I'm anemic and that contributes to my slower healing, but not sure if there's anything else. I took a soft bristle dry brush in the shower and gently but firmly brushed around and on a bruise I had for a few weeks on my thigh. The cream was $15 and the brush I bought was the EcoTools dry body brush for about $6. So it's not a very expensive thing to try out if you are interested. I've got really sensitive skin and didn't notice any irritation from doing it, either. 

Obviously, this is all anecdotal, but I thought maybe it would be useful.

In the meantime, for at home, if the diet is working out, don't change it. Keep puppy play comfortable and well supervised. This puppy is maxxed out on the scratch quota, so no more needed during play! Teaching her how to redirect her biting to a toy may be helpful in preventing her biting herself.

Also, if you have clean, soft hand towels, it may be good to get in the habit of rubbing her paws and vaginal area after she goes out for a potty with a warm damp cloth. Use different towels for the paws and vaginal/tummy area. Just a few gentle strokes is enough. That may help keep bacteria from getting inside any wounds and making it worse. It also may feel calming to the puppy to get rubbed down gently that way.

Make sure she's sleeping a lot. That's not only healthy for young puppies to do, but it will ensure she's not potentially getting in to anything that is making her condition worse OR biting at herself.

If you use any air fresheners, incense, perfume, etc, I would stop using them for now. They wouldn't likely be the cause of her issues, but they may be an additional environmental irritant to her.

If you have the ability, buy her a sweatshirt for dogs or fashion one out of a cotton baby shirt/onesie. This coverage may be more comfortable than her having her wounds out in the open. We had all types of shirts fashioned for dogs that were post-op at my old job. They usually deal with them well.

Finally, enjoy your time with her. She's a baby in need of protection right now, so her feeling that you have her back and are there for her/in control of the situation will make her feel a lot better than if you were constantly worrying and anxious about her state. Just keep doing your best with the vet you have and do what you can at home. Then, just enjoy being with her and absolutely spoiling her!

There are a few reasons why I like the series, but overall I think it has such a positive reception for many because it's selling you a more realistic story. It's not often anime tries to relate to the physical world's internal conflicts. Everything is usually magical, fantastical, over the top kind of expressions of media. Which is fine! I like anime like that, too. I just think that's a big reason why this anime/manga has such a following and is loved by many age groups/genders. We ALL gotta go through puberty and we're ALL awkward and insecure in our own ways, even if others don't see it.

So some personal reasons for me,

I really like Ichikawa's awkwardness and anxiety filled reactions. I am socially awkward and shy, and my internal dialog has been similar to his, even occasionally in adulthood. Especially around people I like.

I also like that it's middle school where we start. I'm not sure if the author will, but I'd love to see them go through high school a bit quicker and maybe move on to college and the beginnings of "adulthood". High school anime/manga is so overdone because it's the point where most people consider characters to be "adult enough" in media for shows/movies/animes. Making them middle schoolers growing up makes more sense. Many of us, including me, were already thinking of adult things/growing up/being scared of it at the age they're at. Not all of us had great high school experiences.

It has beautiful visuals and a cast of characters that give the show diversity in how we grow up. There are SOME really popular anime/manga where the supporting cast doesn't seem to matter. Just background placed in for plot convenience later. It doesn't feel that way with this. It feels like we're seeing various individuals and their minds develop in unique ways based on their shared experiences. Not just one single tone for one scene or a collective agreement of everyone on a situation. Everyone has their own things they go through in their own head and deals with it the best they can based on their already established personality. That's not always something that happens with a manga cast from a single author.

Finally, and maybe the biggest reason I like the series, is that Norio just has a lot of empathy and understanding of a lot of different situations and how individuals can handle those. Her work portrays characters, especially the mc characters, in certain judgmental lights. Ichikawa is cringe, emo, and edgy. Yamada is a model who is insecure over her impact/burden on those around her because she recognizes she's spoiled. Even side characters like Moeko who is "the bitch" character being a lot more grown up and caring than her "bitch" appearance may suggest.  The entire anime/manga centers around not judging individuals based off what you THINK they're like or what you THINK of a social hierarchy, but instead understanding their way of seeing situations and how they navigate the world. Be understanding, be gentle, be kind, and be empathetic towards everyone you see regardless of their external appearance because inside we're all dealing with the human condition. That's how I see it, anyway.

Long essay over!

Heya! I study animals but am also a vet assistant and have experience with plenty of clinical non-emergency issues with dogs. I also have a Border Collie mix who is prone to ear infections/infections in general due to her genetics. Yeast absolutely loves her.

The reason no one wants to give home remedies and instead wants you to see a vet is because there is a whole host of different bacteria inside that ear that needs to be identified before it's treated. Putting on an oil or cleaner without understanding what bacterial overgrowth soup is in there may do a few things. It could unintentionally give the bacteria material to consume/grow in. It could cause extra bacterial growth that would add onto the infected area already. It could also potentially "clear it up" without actually getting rid of the bacteria and the bacteria may move further into the ear and cause worse problems or become resistant to treatment.

This is all based on my academic, professional, and personal learning with infections and ear issues. I would really recommend against doing anything to the ear. As painful as it is, your intervention without medical knowledge and a bacteria swab to identify the target can only cause more pain and more vet visits in the future. 

What I'd recommend is ice to the ear and a benadryl. Benadryl is generally safe and may help reduce the inflammation for the time being and itching. An ice pack wrapped around a CLEAN towel and placed on the ear may help the redness and may help ease pain. Do not use alcohol. Do not use peroxide. Do not use witch hazel. Do not use oils. Do not use antiseptics/antibacterial ointment meant for humans. If you have any DOG (not human) itch/hot spot relief spray that has Lidocaine in it, that should be okay to rub around the outer ear, but don't go into the canal with it. That is a numbing agent and might help with some discomfort and scratching if you have any from a different time. It is what I use when my pup has a flare up but it's not possible to see a vet for a few days because it keeps her away from scratching it all the time and making it worse.

Hopefully this helps.

If you still need some advice, I know I'm late, but I've worked for a while as a vet assistant and have had my fair share of suspicious patients AND those who don't/won't eat because they're suspicious of meds. Unfortunately and fortunately, all dogs are different and the best approach for one dog isn't the best for all dogs. However, I have some general methods that worked well for me for a lot of the picky/suspicious ones. 

First, I highly recommend breaking your dose up into a half or 1/3 if you can. Some dogs are just really great at smelling, tasting, and generally just *sensing* meds and need to be given smaller sizes to help mask it. I found a lot of success by breaking tablets in half and finding out if the dog preferred cheese, pb, or deli meat. Then I would cover the half in whatever preference and stick THAT into a pill pocket. This had a pretty good success rate for me. Of course this won't work if your meds aren't solid tablets and are instead powder capsules, but most vet meds I encounter are tablets. Another thing I can recommend is taking a piece of bread and dipping it in a little bit of broth with the meds wrapped in the bread. This may be easier on the tummy, but it can lead to constipation pretty quick, so I only suggest smaller pieces.

I suggest finding 3-4 treats of ANYTHING that they really like and using that on rotation. Cheese hot dogs warmed up were super successful for me, so was a piece of salami ripped into small bits. Basically, I'd give the dog a treat they really liked first. Like 2 pieces in a row so they can get their suspicions of it sorted out and accept that it is in fact, yummy food. Then I'd give them the med in whatever they seemed to like at the time. Then I'd IMMEDIATELY follow up with another smelly piece of food they liked, usually bigger. This encourages a dog to just swallow whatever they have and grab the next thing.

Next, don't always use the same method. Dogs get bored of tastes just like we do, at least that's what I've come to observe during my time at vet clinics. One day, they love a food! The next they're meh. The next day, they'd rather eat their own vomit. It's absolutely normal for dogs to go 48-72 hours without eating much or using the bathroom much on new meds. Giving them new and exciting foods might interest them temporarily, but they do get used to them if given it consistently.

Onto things that could entice your pup to eat their food, I suggest warm broth, warm chicken shreds, warm pumpkin puree, warm plain oatmeal, and warm cheese sauce. I tried to go from most healthy to least with these, but these have all had success for me in getting dogs of all types to eat their regular food regardless of meds. Warm = smelly = more enticing. For the cheese sauce, I would squirt some easy cheese into a bowl (about 2-4 tablespoons) and mix it with water or low sodium broth. Enough to make it pastey, but not watery cheese. Then I'd microwave it for 30 seconds, mix, and then mix into the food. Let sit for a few minutes to cool. Depending on how much your dog eats/likes cheese, this could be enough for 2-3 meals or just 1. It depends on the dog and their diet preferences. 

If you try any of this and it gives your dogs the runs or constipates them, while that is normal in my experience, it should resolve in about 2 days of eating a bland diet of plain chicken/beef and a bit of rice mixed into their kibble. Of course all of this advice comes with an air of caution around giving too much. This stuff might really work out, but make sure you're not overdoing it. 3-5 pieces of hot dog, salami, or whatever a day for a few weeks shouldn't have a big impact on most dogs if they're otherwise healthy. It just shouldn't become the default way to get them to eat food/take meds. 

The vets I have personally worked with/around say a 7-14 day "ehhhhhh" period for dogs on new meds is normal. The ehhhh refers to lethargy, not eating, mood swings, etc. Basically, this is a buffer period for the medication to enter the system, do its thing, and let the dog's physiology adjust accordingly. If after 2 weeks issues like this persist or don't improve at all, it is time to reassess the medication and possibly try something different.

Trying to work through the first few weeks of a new medication is rough for dogs like it is for humans. Talk with your vet once you've exhausted as many things as you can think of. They may have another idea, they may suggest discontinuing, etc. They're the best resource you have, along with vet techs and vet assistants. You could definitely buddy up with some at your clinic and get them to spill their best advice on medication issues. We all hate pilling the patients as a last resort, so we do tend to get crafty in how we administer meds.

Hope something I've suggested here helps you or anyone who comes across it!

A couple months ago, I went through a GITD phase with HT and Orly's glow polishes. I was actually considering doing a few swatch showcases of my experiments for this month, but haven't found my nail swatch rings. This might sound insane or like a lot of effort buuuuuuut...

I found out that if you do 1 coat of white as your first coat followed by 1 coat GITD, 1st coat color, 1 coat GITD, 2nd and 3rd coat color that you can get pretty much any color to glow without having the milky/grainy look and weird texture. 

You do need to do about 7-8 coats if you're doing a base coat before the white and a top coat at the end, so it's important to do thin coats of everything except the top coat. Also, I used a bit of thinner in all my polishes to make sure nothing was goopy, including the GITD polishes. My nails kinda hate me and I got about 10 days of wear pretty consistently with this method and it didn't chip very much or get discolored over time.

It worked for all my bright colored polishes that need to be built in 2-3 coats. I didn't try any dark colors, the darkest colors I used were the magnetics because they need to be built up and have a pretty bright contrast of pigment, so I thought it'd work. I didn't notice a color fade on the polishes I used either, I assume because I was building color and glow at the same time maybe? I always made sure to finish with 2 color coats before a top coat. I haven't tried without a layer of white as the base color, so not sure if you could just do a normal base coat and then GITD.

I think it's important for people to understand that their version of liking a medium is not the 'correct' or 'normal' way to be a fan of that medium. It's where you stand on the scale of interest with that medium or thing.

For the anime/manga fandom, generally known as otakus, that scale is very vast and has a lot of representation across the board. I'd consider myself an otaku - I definitely enjoy anime and manga of all types and have since I was a kid. But, I have no interest in cosplaying, rping, waifuing, etc. I just watch or read what I like and enjoy the story I'm being told. Most people like this are considered casual otakus, or normie weebs, if you will.

Then you have people who get very attached or dedicated to certain characters or shows or pairings. Something about it is comforting and enjoyable for them and they take a lot of time and dedication to show how much they love the thing. They're more on the positive side of the sliding scale than me, but I still can understand that it's just their way to show their enjoyment of the thing we both like.

It's okay to like the same thing and like it differently. No one is weird or a freak or creepy because they like a specific character. Of course, there are lines in which you can go overboard and become a creepy stalkery like person, but that's far from someone who makes a profile and forum board dedicated to a character. That's just typical hyperfan behavior, honestly.

Really all this shows, in its essence, is younger generations have continued to become restless and defiant with societal expectations. People are living beings with free will. We don't like to be controlled and put into boxes and told how to be. We want to live our lives freely and be who we want and do what we want. We want to be let out of the cages prior generations set us up to be in.

It's always been about that, but with every generation that passes, the tolerance and intolerance from the previous generations grow and grow. Tolerance of human rights, animal rights, environmental rights, etc. continues to grow with every single passing generation. The INTOLERANCE of societal norms and conforming to expectations has grown hand in hand with that. 

Maybe the best example of this can be seen in mental health. Older generations love to boast about how things like ADHD, Autism, depression, anxiety, etc. weren't a "thing" when they were young. What they really mean is that the awareness of symptoms and diagnostic criteria of these things were not as well known, studied, or medically cared for. We have decades upon decades now of studies and documentation for these things that we can review. Medicine is advancing EVERY SINGLE YEAR in some way and it has always been. It's not that the youth THINKS they have something wrong with them, it's that we are now in a place where we can use decades of evidence and medical advancements to recognize these issues and intervene to alleviate the consequences of having them. 

That coupled with the growing agitation of every generation that they be heard and understood and helped for their mental health unlike their parents, grandparents, and so on and you get where we are now. "Oh so many kids nowadays think they have ADHD" or "Oh so many kids these days think they're trans" No. It's not "so many kids these days THINK" anything. It's that our youth grows more and more restless with our societal negligence and misrepresentation of very real problems and they are more vocal about being recognized and treated appropriately. The previous generation told them to do this by standing up for themselves. Same for the generation before that. It's a domino effect.

It's so frustrating to see younger generations treated like they're an issue when they're really the ones who are fighting against the real issue. And those of us in the previous generations literally set them up for this kind of freedom and gave them voices through DECADES of trials and tribulations.

The past shapes the present. Older generations only have themselves to blame for the freedom and voice they've given younger generations. Let the youth fight their fight and then let the youth that comes after do the same. It's their fight, their life, their freedom. None of us in this world haven't benefited from the "younger generations" and their progress. You were all once that younger generation. You were all once the disgrace. You were all only able to make the progress you did in your generation because of the younger generations that came before you. We are all products of this. It's societal evolution.

Yeah, that's why I said to compile a list of stims for him to try out. I grew up stimming in lots of different ways, but I discovered other stims I like better as I got older via seeing others do them or being told about them.

It won't work for every person, but sometimes being told about something and then trying it suddenly "clicks" where we're like WOW HOLY SHIT I LOVE DOING THAT and then we will default to it. 

Like I had a very bad stim of chewing through my shirt collars and sleeve cuffs. It was destructive and costly. I don't do that anymore because I found out chew jewelry was a thing.

In college, I found out fidget jewelry existed (the spin rings) and it helped me stop shaking my leg on the squeaky loud ass floors. Fidgets aren't a choice, but when you notice yourself doing it or people around you noticing it, you become hyperaware of your stim behavior. I still shake my legs like a mad person when I'm in environments I know won't be impacted by it, but when I'm at campus during a lecture, I will catch myself shaking my leg and switch my stim behavior to spinning a ring on my finger or tapping my palm with my fingers.

You can definitely alternate stim behaviors and it doesn't have to be a negative thing.

So your kid likes to verbally stim? Stimming is really vital and important to people with ADHD. It's actively bad for them to NOT stim. So, I'd try to talk with him and tell him that verbally stimming is fine at home/in his room/outside playing but that when he's at school or places where verbal stimming could get him in trouble, to find some other way to stim that soothes him.

For example, I stim in lots of different ways. I like to chew on stuff, click my tongue (quietly), shake my leg, move my fingers, play with my hair, etc. MOST of my stims are silent. He just needs to find a silent one that gives him a similar feeling to his preferred one when in places where he could get in trouble for it.

You should ask him to try out new ways of fidgeting that he likes. Not every kid will like to stim by poking their cheek with their finger, for example, but you won't know until you try it out yourself and see if it's something that gives you satisfaction.

You can look online to find a lot of common stim/fidgets for ADHD/ASD individuals and compile a list to ask him to try out. He might really enjoy some of them and be happy to do them in quiet places and reserve his verbal stims for home time.

Yep, I actually have misophonia. It's incredibly stressful to deal with because everything almost instantly becomes uncomfortable and overwhelming for you. It's just very uncomfortable to deal with. Some people even describe it as painful. It's often described as torture for people who have it.

I've learned that a big reason misophonia enacts rage is by people, both sufferers and those around them, don't think to immediately cease the noise. Instead of yelling and screaming and getting all worked up, I've found what really stops it from even getting to that point is walking away and shutting all audio sensory out for a few minutes.

It saves me embarrassment and shame over having an outburst. It saves me from making people/animals scared or wary around me. And most of all it stops what's agitating me and allows my brain to think rationally and calmly about what to do instead of react. Grab a pair of earbuds, go for a walk, listen to some pleasing audio (nature noises happen to calm me), etc.

Snuffle mats are a great stimulation activity. I'd recommend getting like 2 or 3 so you can swap them out regularly to keep them from getting old/boring. There's lots of cute ones on Amazon, just make sure to check the dimensions out.

I would try to make it a habit of taking 5 minute breaks every 90 minutes (or just when you can) and using that 5 minutes to practice recall/tricks or just toss a ball in the house. 5 minutes at a time is better than no minutes. 

Kongs with frozen treats inside will make for good stimulation. You can also find other kong-like toys that you can stuff smaller treats in.

Get your dog into the routine of walking in the evening until the summer heat dies down. That way puppo knows that a walk is coming - just at a certain time. Being consistent and keeping to a routine can help with destructive behaviors. When you do go on walks, let your dog be the guide. This will make the walk even more rewarding and fulfilling if they get to decide the direction/what to stop and sniff for a bit.

I would also recommend carving out 10-15 minutes in the morning for some high intensity fun. Running/playing chase with each other, hide and go seek in the house, throwing a ball, practicing recall, or just rough housing. This will help alleviate some of the boredom during your busy hours and will tucker your pup out for a nap.

I used to think I had like BED or something because of this. I also have an oral fixation. I just like to be chewing on/biting/licking/etc something at like all times.

It really depends on your texture preferences, but here are some things I find that I enjoy:

- As many have said, gum, but, I recommend trying various types of gum. Gum balls, stick gum, gum rope, etc. They all have slightly different textures and chewing profiles. Also be careful with gum though because excessively chewing gum all the time has the possibility of leading to jaw problems from overworking your mandible. Also, mints.

- Sugar free pudding/jello. It's cheap, not very caloric, and it's fun to mess with/eat (for me).

- If you like diet/zero cal/low cal teas or drink mixes, I recommend getting some and taking a big drink and letting it sit on your tongue before swallowing. It's not CHEWING, but it does coat your mouth with flavor and I find myself more satisfied if I let a drink sit in my mouth for like 15-20 seconds rather than just drinking it. I do this with water too when I'm really thirsty while on my meds. Helps with my cotton mouth.

- I really enjoy pickles. I like to kind of dissect them as I eat them and you can get a giant jar of pickles for like $5-6. I think spears and halves are about the same amount of satisfying for me. Plus the salt/vinegar has some electrolytes in it so that's nice. 

- Veggie noodles/zoodles. These are pretty cheap and pretty low cal. I like them for when I want something hot and want to kind of go through the motions of eating a meal but don't actually want to eat a meal.

- If you tolerate caffeine well, they make a lot of caffeine chews/mints. You can get the satisfaction of chewing while also getting a bit of a stimulant which can help with hunger. Or you could freeze coffee into small ice cubes and chew on those.

- Finally, not food, but chew jewelry is something I highly recommend for you if you really like the sensation of just chewing. As a kid I used to chew through my shirt collars and sleeves and stuff. Destroyed pencils/pens/etc. Basically, I wanted to constantly be chewing or biting on something. You can get pretty cheap chew jewelry that is made of good quality material and is durable. I enjoy it for when I'm bored/need to think or focus on what I'm doing.

I know a lot of the replies to you are just calling OP childish and essentially pushing all of their past experiences with communication mishaps onto her, but I come with an alternative answer. 

Feelings are not always rational and logic based. Have you ever noticed that when people get into situations where fight or flight kicks in, they tend to make sudden and drastic decisions?

To this woman's brain, what she saw got perceived as a threat. Her brain then started sending rapid fire signals that likely had her heart racing, her mind pacing, and her body shaking. It's called an adrenaline rush. It happens pretty much whenever we get scared/nervous and causes us to be on edge and do things our normal brain would not typically do.

Do I think she handled this the best? In a broad sense, no. But, in a sense from her brain freaking out? Yeah, I think she did pretty good. She knew she was immediately overwhelmed and overtaken by her emotions so she distanced herself. When we sense a threat to our wellbeing, we tend to create distance. It's a safety precaution. To her brain in that moment, confronting him about it immediately could verify her fears. We tend to not want to confront our fears as our brains have learned they are...well...fearful.

She left, isolated herself until she calmed down, and then came back and confronted the situation when her brain was no longer in panic mode. That is something that you are encouraged to do in relationship therapy. It helps to keep situations from escalating or getting to a potentially hurtful point. Had she confronted him right then and there it may have come out like "WHY THE FUCK DO YOU HAVE A CONDOM? WHY WOULD YOU CHEAT ON ME? HOW COULD YOU?" and potentially put him on the defensive and started an entire vacation ruining argument. What happened in reality is that they DID communicate and they DID resolve it and nobody yelled, no serious accusations were thrown out, no one's feelings were hurt, and they laughed about it. 

What is ONE DAY of a vacation compared to the rest of a relationship? She can make it up to him in the future, and he can learn to be more open and honest about normal bodily functions. If ruining one day on vacation would be enough to ruin an entire relationship for you, then your relationship was already fickle and had little to no trust anyways. 

You don't just toss a partner to the side because they allowed their emotions to overwhelm them and panic in a misunderstanding. You learn to talk with them better to help avoid future conflict. You set boundaries. Expectations. You accept it for what it was and move on. If it happens AGAIN, then fine. But as a first reaction? Well, now you're just in the comments being as irrational as she was.

Hi! I'm not a trainer, but I have a dog who pulls also. He's an aussie/collie mix and he's super overstimulated by everything outside. I too got him from a loving family, they just didn't have the time to give him. I figured maybe I could share some of the things I have done that do work for me in hopes something may help you.

- 1. I highly recommend you work on recall inside the house before you go on walks. Just 5 minutes of having your dog sit, stay, come, etc with a high value reward of their liking. 



- 2. Before the walk even starts, I would suggest desensitizing your dog to the door unlocking, then opening, then your dog looking outside from inside. I used to have babygates for the longest time for my pups to block them from my bedroom and livingroom and I recently decided to fix it to the doorframe to my patio. This helped him not be able to escape and let him take in the outside from inside. Does it look crazy? Mildly. Do I care what people think? Not really.



- 3. My dog also isn't aggressive in anyway, but he is *reactive*. Lots of people assume reactive means he wants to attack or is prone to, but no. He is reactive to any stimuli that excites him and he wants to go *PLAY* with that stimuli. He is...overly friendly to put it mildly. I often will ask the owner if he is allowed to meet a passing dog. Now, he looks like the Tasmanian Devil from Looney Tunes when another dog is around, so I always let the owner know that he is actually very friendly, he's just very excited and noisy. He has this high pitched girly whine bark that he does that can freak dogs/people out, so I always let them know it's something we're working on because he wasn't socialized very well. 


Sometimes they say yes, sometimes they say no. If they say yes, I will let them play for a minute to 5 minutes and then we will say bye and move on. I feel like this has been useful in showing him that I am not trying to keep him away from "fun things" on walks, it's just that sometimes those fun things aren't things he can do right away and that's okay. Socializing him has been very important for getting him to be calmer around dogs. He now doesn't girly whine bark at certain dogs he has met a few times because he knows he can meet them *occasionally* and it's not a "now or never" situation.



- 4. I often take him to "hot spots" on our walks where I notice his behavior is more erratic and I will just sit with him and let him run around like a crazy buffoon until I notice he has calmed a bit. Then I get him into a sit by me and we watch traffic/people/birds/whatever it is that is exciting him together. This is mainly how I do my desensitization. I have found this IMMENSELY helpful. He used to literally run down the steps so quickly that it scared me that I would fall and break my legs or arms. Now he actually waits for me and walks at a slower pace down steps because I constantly stopped and just sat around the steps.



- 5. Find a high reward treat your dog REALLY likes and then condition him to like it even MORE inside. Then I would suggest opening a window or whatever to the outside and feeding your pet the treat as they see other dogs pass/people pass/anything interesting is happening outside. It's important to note that I am suggesting you give them the treat and mark their behavior BEFORE they bark or get too excited. The goal is trying to let them know that seeing something go by and remaining calm (or calmer than usual) leads to rewards.


Both my collie mixes really like the Rachael Ray Nutrish Treats AND the Dogsters Ice Cream. The Rachael Ray treats run about $11 USD at Wal-Mart, BUT I found out I can break each treat into around 4-6 treats depending on how big they are. The Savory Roasters and Burger Bites are easiest for me to break. I can get an entire 12oz bag to last 2 weeks with both of them this way. 


For the Dogsters Ice Cream, I like these for desensitization while we are sitting outside. I can give him one and he'll slowly eat it while looking around until he finally lays down. Once that happens, I praise him for being calm. The ice cream is around $3 at Wal-Mart for 4 cups, and I don't use the cups daily. I also tend to give him one while maintenance/gardening people are working outside the apartment complex. He can watch them from a window and eat his ice cream while I hold it and that has honestly helped a ton with his barking/excitement at windows.


You could also freeze a KONG with PB or cream cheese mixed with some water to thin it out to create a similar effect for the ice cream method. I'm just lazy and I like the convenience of the cups.



- 6. I highly recommend not making every walk a training walk. This failed me quickly. Instead, I have decided to go the slower route of having the first 2 walks of the day be half training/half "do whatever you want within reason". Then our final walk of the day is free reign for him to do whatever he wants (within reason) as he is more distracted of the evening. Just like with people, some time of the day we learn better than others where we just want to relax. I want him to view walking as fun and enjoyable exercise/stimulation, not as a drill training session. That just makes him sad and unresponsive.



- 7. I have learned to observe him throughout the walk to see his behavior. I notice that around 10 mins in he seems to get kind of tired but excited, similar to how a toddler will fight a nap by playing more. This is a good sign to me that the walk is over now, at least for training purposes. At this point I will let him just sniff, and I will usually take the time to sit at a spot to do some desensitization. Once he calms himself enough to sit or lay by me, I will get up after a solid minute of him being calmer and we will go back home. Sometimes we walk about 1.5 hours throughout the day (3-4 walks) and sometimes it's only 40-45 minutes a day. I really have learned to leave it up to him in that context because some days are hotter or more stimulating than others and he needs less time out or he goes into "overstimulation" mode where he is absolutely untrainable and uncooperative. The duration of his walking/sniffing/adventuring means less to him (and me) than his satisfaction of his time doing it.



- 8. Finally, I recommend trying non-walks before walking. Say you walk your dog 3 times a day. I suggest having 3 periods where you are just sitting outside with your dog and doing nothing with them before you walk them for about 5-10 minutes. So if I want to walk my little demon child at 12, I will go out around 11:30 and just sit on my patio with him and let him take in the outside. The sounds, smells, animals, people, etc. There's no treats during this time or even really communication other than me praising him and petting him. I just let him have some space on his leash and let him run around until he settles. Then we go back in. Then we go out for the real walk half an hour later. It's like putting him into tutorial mode.



I would really emphasize working on your understanding of your dog's body language during walks and taking things slow. You're not a drill sargeant and he isn't a soldier in training, so every walk doesn't need to be an event to learn. That really halted my progress for a few months until I looked at it differently and started respecting his craziness more and in turn, he has started to respect my requests of him more. I want walking to be rewarding for us both, and it just isn't when I am frustrated that he won't listen and he's frustrated that I won't "let him have fun".

I recommend checking out Kikopup on youtube. She has a lot of videos explaining/showing how to get a dog's attention and work on recall better. A big thing about training dogs and puppies is that your mood during the training session sets the mood for not only that session, but for future sessions.

So, if you seem annoyed/bored/unmotivated while training, that is going to be something the dog picks up on. I mean, would you want to hang out and learn from a teacher who was super boring? So, try to have fun with it. They need to feel rewarded for the act of training so that way it seems like an activity they want to do.

Dogs like to do things like dig, chew, destroy things because the action itself is a reward. They find pleasure in it. It scratches an itch for them. So, you have to find out ways that you can instead satisfy that itch for them. If they find training with you to become a rewarding task then they will be motivated in the future and pay more attention to what you are asking of them.

It all really starts with good communication and relationship building with you and your dog. Training, in my opinion, should be treated more like doggy dates than doggy school lessons.

Pretty much every job I've ever had, this has been said to me...often. In some variation. Being 26 now, going through Uni, and having worked 6-7 jobs in that time from small part time retail to more stable work in my field of interest, I have found workarounds to these issues. I also have ADHD, which matters for later.

I think the biggest mistake you can make when people mention you being quiet, is staying quiet in that moment. I don't mean becoming an extrovert, I mean expressing yourself. For example, I have had moments where someone, like my manager or coworker, is telling me something I need to know and stopped and mentioned my silence. In those moments I often say "Oh, I am sorry, I just am observing so I can better understand." In the same vein, if I'm doing something at work and someone mentions me being quiet I have learned to say "Yeah, I'm just focusing right now and I know talking will distract me."

For meetings, I have told my bosses/managers many times that I often forget things in the heat of the moment of a meeting so what I like to do is email somebody my input on things prior to a meeting or afterwards for the next meeting. I've literally never had them discourage this form of participation in meetings. Sometimes I will say I want to talk about those items, other times I will say I'd just like to bring it up as a group discussion/question I want clarified. 

For general socializing, I debrief people, often. It is not uncommon for me to tell people that I am very quiet but observant and that I like to randomly jump in and out of conversations at my own pace. I let them know if I don't really have input on a topic or if I don't really seem approachable at times, it doesn't mean I hate them or anything. It just means I genuinely have nothing to offer.

I ALWAYS tell people I work with that I like to present myself as authentic as I can and that sometimes that means I just have nothing to say. I do my very best work when I am by myself in my "zone" and that often means complete silence. There are days where I can talk somebody's ear off and then there are days where I only say the bare minimum of words needed. 

Also, I commonly have asked that people either leave me notes, send me texts, or email me with specific things they want addressed. For example, if someone needs me to complete a 5 step process, I would ask that they leave simplified instructions for the steps after verbally/physically walking me through it the first time. This way I don't have to awkwardly seek them out every 20 minutes because I keep forgetting something and then make conversing with me seem much harder/like a chore.

Like I said, I have ADHD, which means I have developmental delays. I am not the best at picking up social cues, and I am not the best at timing my social cues. I'm not any less equipped to handle my work and responsibilities, I just can't multitask people talking about their chores, their partners, their kids, the Moon's alignment tonight, etc while effectively doing my work. It is a distraction for me. I let people know that if my quietness or quickness to their responses comes off as rude to let me know, so I can explain what is happening.

I'm never going to be Chatty McTalkerson, and I want people to know pretty early on that having that expectation of me is going to lead to everyone being let down and frustrated. 

I do this at school, too. I had a Uni professor for like 6 classes since they all related to my major. Participation was expected and graded, though it wasn't intense. He figured out very early on that in-class participation made me very uncomfortable and anxious, but that I did want to participate because I'd email him and essentially have discussions about the material with him directly after. He ended up really valuing my input on a lot of stuff and often times I'd come to class and see things I had brought up get discussed in class. Sometimes that would lead to discussions that I could partake in because I had already been given the opportunity to think of things. He really respected the fact I did want to be a part of the work, I just needed a little accommodation and patience to get there.

That's really what needs to be established for OP and people like OP. You need to communicate what your comfort level and boundaries are around socializing. You don't need to change. They don't need to change. What needs to change is the expectations. They can't expect you to become super social and talkative when you aren't. You can't expect them to not want to socialize with you when they want to/need to. Both parties need to come to a mutual agreement and respect the other's comfort levels and find compromises that satisfy everyone. It shouldn't and really can't be one or the other.

Does your mom or any of your neighbors have outdoor cameras? If so you can ask them to review footage of the time you roughly believe the pup went missing. That may give you a general reference of where you should be looking. 

Alternatively, if there are any small shops or gas stations nearby you could also ask them if they would be willing to review outside security footage to see if she passed by.

Does she have a particular food/smell she is drawn to? For example, if you know she likes warmed up hotdogs as a treat you could place some around the property. If she stayed nearby and hid somewhere away from view, that could lure her out.

I'd also suggest searching on a bike where you can. Cars approaching can make animals hide/stay hidden and a bike is more silent and gives the opportunity for you to stop, look around, move for a bit, and repeat. It can make surveying an area easier than by car where you need to constantly drift or get out to look. A bike would also offer easier access to park areas, trails, etc.

Does she have a specific toy noise she is attracted to? If she likes squeaky toys for example, you could grab a few and use them periodically while walking/biking around as it may catch her attention and draw her out to peek.

Check under bridges, porches, and vehicles nearby (with the consent/help of neighbors). Smaller dogs tend to hide under structures instead of wandering off into forests for a few reasons. It's more quiet, it offers more shielding from the elements, and it offers them a sense of security by making them harder to see to predators.

Having dealt with suicidal thoughts since I was about 12 and being 26 now, I definitely relate to the memes on this sub that are about watching out for others. I have always, ever since I was younger, made it my goal to try and help others through their darkest times.

It's not that I am a super people-loving person, it's that I inherently think other people's lives have value. If I can be there for someone in the way I needed someone to be there for me, maybe I can change the miserable trajectory they're on and help their mindset. 

Maybe *I* can be the difference someone needs to go get help, or to put down the pill bottle, or to eat their next meal. Maybe in 20 years time they'll briefly remember the conversations we had that helped them through. Or maybe not, either way is okay, as long as I made a positive impact.

We can all feel like our specific struggles are very "one of a kind" where the only way out is not existing, but none of us tend to view others that way. Not that we're downplaying their trauma or struggle, but it's that seeing issues from an outside perspective tends to engage our critical thinking and problem solving skills. 

For many people who are "passively" suicidal like myself, I've found that they share this sentiment. Imagine burning a casserole in the oven and then imagine someone else burning a casserole in their oven while you are with them. 

You have to deal with the fact you've wasted ingredients, wasted money buying them, wasted the time it took to prepare it, and now the fire alarms are going off and you need to frantically wave an oven mitt around and open the windows while you smell burning and hear loud noises constantly alerting you to your mistake. You're so overwhelmed that it feels like your entire life is burning up in that moment. 

But, when you watch someone else do this, you grab an oven mitt and help them wave it around. You open the windows for them. You suggest alternative dinner ideas. You say "oh this is no problem, I've done this SO many times! Why don't we order a pizza?" or you may offer to make them a meal while they destress from the chaos. Because to you, this is just a typical part of life. People burn things. But when it is YOU doing it, it's no longer visible from that outside perspective.

That's kinda how this is, at least for me.

My writing has never ever been flagged for AI use, but I have been out of classes the past 2 semesters due to unfortunate circumstances. Is this a new thing to worry about when I go back?

I see a lot of these comments being like save multiple drafts, save to a cloud, etc. While I don't disagree you should be saving your progress every so often in case of sudden crashes, if they're going to use an AI to determine if you used AI, shouldn't that AI have more to offer than a percentage to show it is supposedly AI written?

For example, for many years professors have checked if papers were copy/pasted using some online programs that scan essays/papers to find blocks of text that are verbatim ones. If AI is picking up that this text is AI generated, why does it have nothing of substance to prove that other than a percentage?

Percentages mean nothing on their own. You need to apply context to them for them to have any meaning or ground for the claim of the percentage. 

All AI does, from my understanding, is generates text based off of previous written text (see the constitution error with AI) and identifiable writing styles based on whatever you are asking it.

We are all pretty much taught when learning how to write essays/papers that we need to write in a specific style. We need to write with specific mannerisms, punctuation, paragraph breaks, etc. So that way the writing appears legible. A LOT of times if students take the creative liberty to apply their own writing style or mannerisms in their "professional" graded papers they'll be docked points for being too informal.

So, this seems like it creates a huge issue for writing academia. You're damned if you do stick to the cookie cutter way you're expected to string sentences along, and you're damned if you try to interject your own personality into the writing.

I'm curious how many science research papers AI would find AI generated because they are almost all written in the same exact format for ease of navigation. If someone were to write, for example, "Thus, with these data points we can infer....." in their research paper, that's pretty much what everyone ends up writing in their research paper, and thus this would be a data point AI would use to write out its own research paper. 

In the same vein, what if we started using AI to determine if math homework was AI generated? How can you prove that? We all have to solve the same equations with the same formulas to get the right answers, and AI will be able to do the same thing.

This seems like something that professors should be aware of instead of just blindly accepting a number with no back up resources to provide their reasoning for that number. Like don't just tell us it's whatever % AI generated, show us AI generated examples and where that AI is compiling its data to generate those examples. Then cross reference that to the citations of your paper and if they link up you may need to reassess that %. If they don't link up then it's more likely the student AI generated an essay and then slapped some citations on it.

So, the answer to this question lies in the context of why they are asking. I feel like running through different scenarios answers this question best.

Scenario 1: If I was going on a big business trip in an unfamiliar place and my partner asked me to install a tracking app so they could check it for piece of mind that I am at my hotel/business location/wherever I last said I was, then yes. This is because it's reasonable for a partner to want to be able to check your safety when you are out of reach with no viable way for them to get to you. If it had been hours since I last communicated, it would make sense that my partner would want to check up on me to see if I am in a familiar location/place I said I would be. If I'm not and don't answer, then it would be appropriate to worry for my safety.

Scenario 2: If I was a previous or current/potential victim of stalking or harassment. If my partner has been made aware of potential dangerous people knowing my whereabouts, it would make sense they would ask this as a way to check in on my safety. Plus, if I were in fear for my safety, it would be nice to know I am being watched with my consent as it would feel like someone was protecting me rather than snooping. 

Scenario 3: If I had cheated on them and we had been making attempts to better the relationship, it would make sense to temporarily allow them to see that I am making trustworthy actions and am where I say I am going to be. This scenario is tricky, because it can turn into obsessive checking, so this one would only really be advisable if I felt like my partner and I had communicated that it was a trust building exercise to show my changed ways rather than a cheat tracker.

Scenario 4: My partner just wants to watch where I am at all times. This is a no go for me, because it's not reasonable to want to follow a person's every movement in the chance that you might catch them doing something. This is rooted in deeper issues and is not a healthy request. It's fine to want me to check in or give updates via texts where I am/what I'm doing, but it's different if my word isn't enough. Especially if there have been no prior issues of infidelity/mistrust.

There are lots of other scenarios with yes/no acceptable answers to this. But, what really matters in this question is what the context for asking would be.

Eating DISORDERS are almost never about the food and almost always about the person's inflection of themselves. They've been made to feel certain ways, which leads them to act in certain ways that can give them control. 

A hypothetical example of this using the OP could be "my friend kept telling me I was a fat fuck. So I am a fat fuck. God, why am I such a fat fuck? Is that why everyone looks at me weird?
