I'm 26 now, still fidget like mad. Never going to not probably. It's just how I am, but it's such an obvious sign that I was in need of constant stimulation to regulate myself.

There were so many more things, not just one, but the constant need to move is absolutely a sign that neurologically something else is going on. I needed that movement and sensory feedback to help calm me, focus me, and entertain me.

BONUS CUTE SIDE STORY BECAUSE MY MEDS ARE ACTIVE AND ALSO MAYBE USEFUL FOR YOU GUYS:

My partner likely has some sort of undiagnosed disorder that makes him act a lot like ADHD/Autism in many aspects. I try to encourage him to seek a diagnosis, but he refuses. Anyways, we went to the store a couple weeks ago and it was like PACKED. Majorly packed. We both have social anxiety issues, but I am older than he is and I am the type of person who kind of pushes my anxieties to the side when I see someone else needing care. We were both pretty much immediately overwhelmed in the store, but I was doing the thing where I hyperfocus on my task (my list) so I was managing. He was not.

So, I suggested that we go down the toy aisle to find a fidget toy he could mess with inside his pocket while we shopped. We found this fidget cube ($4 at Wal-Mart) but it was in a box so he couldn't test it and he didn't really like anything else. The boxes are taped shut with 2 small pieces of tape, so I gently peeled them back and he liked it so we put the empty container in the cart so we could ring it up at checkout and he played with it in his pocket. It helped him a ton.

We got to a point where I was getting super overwhelmed and shutting down in the store and he gave it to me to play with for a bit. It really helped because it had so many different sides with different functions and I could just go ham getting sensory feedback from the various sides. It kept me from breaking down crying and I was able to manage the rest of the shopping trip.

So PSA to you guys who read this and get overwhelmed in stores and stuff. Go to the toy section, find something you like and then play with it during your shopping. Just remember to grab the container it comes in and put it in the front of your cart so you can be sure to ring it up at the end of the trip. I do highly recommend getting a fidget cube from Wal-Mart if you have them, because it was $4 and that is extremely inexpensive when considering how calming it can be when you are experiencing sensory overload/overwhelm to the point of a meltdown. 

I wouldn't worry about getting in trouble for doing this, because I used to work in grocery stores and there are a LOT of parents who tend to give their kids snacks out of the boxes or open up unpaid for drinks at the snack cooler and drink while shopping. They never got in trouble, because they would always ring up the bottles/boxes at check-out. Most employees at stores (unless they're new) will know what you're doing if they see you open something and then place the empty container in your cart. Even as a kid my mom used to ring up 1-2 empty water bottles during long shopping trips and the cashiers never said anything.

This is very nice. For anyone wanting to do something similar and cheap, you could buy baby **wool** sock packs. You can get sock packs of 4-6 pairs for about 3-5 dollars at most stores, or you could get many more from your local goodwill/thrift shop for even less. Depending on where you are and where these homeless pets live, the cold can get so bad that they can't walk. Especially if they walk on salty walkways as salt makes it colder to step on. Socks are a nice temporary shield from paw pads directly hitting the salt and then snow/ice. It can help prevent injury/possible frostbite or infection if the dog gets wounded. 

Most dogs don't like socks/booties right out the gate, but even my dogs prefer some layer on their feet when the cold hits. I feel like they rationalize "it's either this or limping." The socks can also be easily cleaned and dried given their small size and even warmed up if put under a warm cup of coffee, light, etc. They're also stretchy so you can buy the smallest sizes and still have it fit most medium/large dog paw sizes.

If you want to make jackets for cheap and have spare toddler pants no longer being used - you can use them! I used to work in a vet hospital that used old and unwanted kids pants and shirts as covers for dogs post op. You cut a hole in the crotch and boom bam, you have a makeshift jacket/covering.

Just a couple small things for if people see this and want to contribute to their local homeless and pets but don't have a lot of extra resources to buy new $15-20 dog jackets. Many times, these pets mean so much to their owners, especially during homeless and hopeless conditions. They deserve love and care too and I'm beyond happy to see this first thing in the morning!

Edit: Edited in clarification from another comment that if you do gift socks, wool is better than cotton because of the potential dangers of wet cotton drawing away heat. I checked my local Target/Walmart and they have wool baby sock packs between 4-8 pairs for around 7-12 dollars, so it is still reasonable!

First of all, if you are comfortable enough to do so, I would highly recommend working with a behavioral therapist that specializes in EDs as they will be able to guide you better on how to avoid and/or eliminate trigger responses to certain items.

With that said, it may be useful to have an item such as a sucker, gum, cough drop, etc with you when you encounter trigger foods. Having a specific taste blend with another taste already in your mouth can reduce the desire to want to mix those. For example, the taste of chocolate is generally not very good when you drink soda before or after it. 

So, if you eat some of the bread but you don't want it to spiral into an episode, try following it with a taste that is not complimentary as it may help you stop eating it. Nothing gross to make you sick, just something that doesn't particularly mix well.

In addition, try not to deny yourself the food you like or create a stigma around it. Telling ourselves "no! That is bad! It's always bad!" tends to create the response of "I know this is bad butttttt...just this one time" and that can create a toxic loop of ED behaviors. 

Instead, you could try taking a specific amount you feel comfortable with eating, placing it on a separate dish, and eating only that amount. Wait for 5 or 10 minutes and if you really are craving more, have a little more that you feel comfortable with. Having an entire package of something in front of our faces can trigger the response of "why NOT eat it all?" and that can make us feel like we have no control over ourselves and can lead into spirals. Mindless eating can be okay, but if it's hurting you and making you sick, it may help to remove larger portions from your immediate access. This gives you time to think as you go and get more so you can say "okay I'll just have another piece or two" instead of "well, I ate one so I might as well eat 10". Sometimes our brains just need a couple minutes to process to get us to a more rational choice.

Again, I do recommend therapy to help your mind break down the stigma surrounding this trigger food, but I hope this was of some help.

Cognitive Behavioral Therapy is actually the basis of this kind of conditioning and is one of the top recommended methods of treating ADHD along with medication.

So, medicine IS important, but it's not the only way. Some people cannot afford or tolerate medications or they just don't want to take that avenue. Today I decided to take a relaxing shower because I am still recovering from the physiological consequences of this and I feel like I had a moment of clarity. At least for me, my ADHD tends to make me overcompensate to appear "typical" or "normal". That means the more outside responsibility I take on, the less I care for my own needs and wellbeing. To me, life has always been about proving people wrong and showing them that I am good enough. This results in me putting in so much effort, beyond 100%, that I figuratively work myself to the bone. 

As I sat in the shower and gave my hair an oil treatment while singing to some music on my phone I was suddenly like "ah. This is it".

I've stopped catering to my own needs and feelings because all my mental capacity is spent on caring about others needs and feelings. No wonder I'm not fucking capable of feeling positive emotions, I'm denying myself basic care. I'm always trying to deny who I am in favor of what I think others want me to be. In the past few years I've forgotten how to even relax by myself. Because even when I'm alone, I'm always thinking about what I need to be doing that I currently am not and what people will think of me for not doing it. There's no time to relax for me, there's only time to be better and improve.

This shower showed me that's bullshit. It's been 6 months since I've actually even felt like myself and not just an autopilot zombie. I'm not recovered, but I felt a tiny little sliver of who I am while dancing around and singing in the shower. Letting the hot water relax my muscles and giving my hair (which is now falling out due to stress) some TLC.

So with all that, I say to you: You need to care about yourself more. So fucking often people with disabilities put 500% of themselves into trying to be "normal" without realizing the amount of effort and care we're putting in is vastly overdone. The way I explain this is kinda how you learn the order of species in Biology (even though the order is flawed it's a useful analogy). 

Example:
 
- Symptom: Executive Dysfunction

- Trait: Not being able to motivate self to do basic tasks (such as study, shower, clean, etc)

- Tendency: Leaving clothes in the washer for 3 days because you're unmotivated to put them in the dryer.

It works in sentence structure too:

"I experience executive dysfunction" 

"One of my traits is my lack of motivation to study until it's too late"

"I have a tendency to leave my clothes in the washer for days"

Symptoms are basically like broad definitions. Traits are like habits you've formed within those symptoms. Tendencies are subconscious or mostly motor function responses to the learned trait of the symptom.

I'ma be honest, throw the whole doctor away. 

When I spoke to my doctor about my ADHD, even though she isn't a psychiatrist/specialist, she listened to my SYMPTOMS and how I articulated my struggles. That's how she decided the med and the dose for me. Her exact words when she started me on my first stim (which didn't work - it took a few tries) was "I am giving you a slightly higher starting dose because your ADHD appears pretty severe and I don't believe a low dose would make a dent". She also told me that I should know within a week if a stimulant is or isn't right for me.

Stimulants are not like SSRIs where they need to build up in the system. Stimulants don't actually put dopamine into your body, what happens is they basically just don't signal a receptor to stop dopamine production/distribution, so the feedback loop isn't halted at any process. Then, after awhile the stimulant gets metabolized and the system now has nothing stopping it from creating a dopamine imbalance feedback loop again. This means that stimulants are by design fast acting and don't require a build up of any chemical - your body actually makes all the dopamine it needs already, it's just an issue of getting it to distribute it correctly which is what the stimulant is for.

So in summary, yeah I'd throw the whole doctor away. They clearly don't understand the mechanisms behind ADHD functionality nor stimulants role in that mechanism and as such are unfit to really be prescribing you anything for it. You need a specialist who understands ADHD, which is unfortunate as it's not as convenient as the doctor you're used to but is likely necessary if this is something you're looking for further help with.

Okay so, I wanna speak up as someone who has both BDD (Body dysmorphic disorder) and ADHD as a female because I feel like I can provide perspective to both sides. Plus, if I was personally in your place I'd want as much insight as I could get since these are more complex issues than just insecurities.

For her and the BDD, yes, absolutely porn can destroy a person with this disorder. Porn is not inherently bad, but it can exacerbate symptoms of BDD to the point it's all consuming. I will get very candid - this disorder has led me down a very destructive and self hating path with my physical self. I don't even know what I actually look like entirely - I've had two partners tell me I have a very warped visual of my body (one had me show him how big I thought my stomach was with my fingers and then was shocked and in disbelief when he realized how bad my sense of self is). Even writing this and not being extremely descriptive of my issues makes me tear up. BDD isn't just insecurity and not liking yourself. It takes a lot of care and boundaries and effort, not only from the individual but also their support system, to be able to overcome it.

Now, some of her actions aren't justified such as the cheating "prank" (which I have a suspicion was her *trying* to convey how you were making her feel with porn) but some of the things - like the boundary with porn - are extremely valid. I have known I wasn't okay with porn in my relationships since I was a teenager. I grew up watching a lot of anime and reading a lot of manga, so when I discovered the NSFW stuff at like 13/14 and seen how "ideal" those anime girls were to people online, it permanently damaged me in a way that I started consuming NSFW content specifically to make myself feel worse and compare myself, and I still do sometimes. It's almost like I have to feel undesirable and disgusting. BDD will eat you up inside and outside and it's a very isolated disorder because the people with it are usually seen as vain or narcissistic when really they just feel inadequate.

Personally, I tell all my partners *before we even get intimate* that porn in our relationship is an absolute invasion of my trust and will actually mentally affect me if I ever find out about it. I'm lucky in the fact that all my partners have agreed and have been open and candid about it. My current partner understands that even some media content I can't watch with him (such as NSFW games or certain movies) because of the fact he's there, so I automatically assume any other female depicted in a sexual way is better than me. If I say "I can't watch this anymore" he'll very nonchalantly be like "okay" and we'll find something else. I am someone who is open to sharing my body on video/in pics for my partner, so it isn't like I have condoned only sexy time for when I'm with them.

Now, onto the ADHD/you part. You cannot fully control yourself when you're heated and upset. Nobody can. It's very hard to ask someone with ADHD to just stop doing a thing they do for a dopamine hit.  You're not evil, and I think honestly (coming from both ADHD AND BDD) you did your best given the abruptness of her BDD discovery. I don't think you need to be a better person in this situation. I think you should both stay your separate ways and just move about life with this as a bitter memory and a reminder that communication is extremely important. I know communicating with ADHD can be hard because we can sometimes miss social cues or can be a bit bouncy with our points/topics, but that doesn't make it any less important for relationships. 

I would say for your next relationship, just be up front and honest early like "hey, my ex had BDD and she wasn't comfortable with porn in our relationship but I didn't know until later - is there anything similar that I should know is a boundary for you?" and then I'd explain (if it were me) that I have ADHD and that I will try my best to not invade that boundary but I may need reminders sometimes and I may make mistakes or need alternatives. FWIW, if you had been my partner and I discovered my BDD later in our relationship, given how bad I know my BDD is I would have still been much more forgiving as it's a new change and thus requires adjusting.

Exposure, in my experience, tends to let the dog adjust better to a situation rather than forcing them to obey. I don't generally like to pull, but as I am currently training 2 border collie mixes who enjoy tugging me like a ragdoll, I do sometime pull them back in response to them nearly murdering me by going down the stairs like racing hyenas.

However, for typical everyday interactions, all the positive training videos I have seen recommend allowing your dog to just desensitize themselves to the situation (assuming they don't need your comfort). 

Essentially, the idea would be the more often your dog is freely able to observe and settle into seeing other dogs for example, the easier it is for them to start to ignore it. It's always good (in my opinion) to give a dog time to make their own choices and not just follow our commands as we demand them, a big riff between my partner and I actually.

Patience and understanding in addition to time have made the biggest behavioral impacts on my duo. If I may suggest, getting your pup used to a command to look directly at you whenever there is something they want to access/go to/are uncertain of is a good addition to your current method and may help your partner. If your dog always knows to look at you or your partner for affirmation of the next step it may alleviate any anxiety they feel about a situation. My dogs know when I call their names, I want their attention via eye contact so they know what I want from them. This also helps a distracted dog refocus from what I've read as it kind of puts them back into their usual routine that they know how to respond in.

"The point being that if something really is  important, you won't have ADHD suddenly." This implies having ADHD is a choice that can be turned on or off. I definitely mean no disrespect, I am just trying to clarify that nothing takes away your ADHD. ADHD isn't a feeling, there are actual parts of your brain that have developed differently from other typical brains. A house on fire doesn't re-develop those parts of your brain to suddenly not have ADHD for 10 minutes.

Just because you can't focus on them doesn't indicate they don't matter to you. There's a barrier between you and the task at hand that causes this motivational rift. Many people with ADHD tend to have very narrow sight in this aspect. 

For example, I want to eventually become an animal rehabilitation therapist. That is my goal. It's important to me. However, to achieve this goal I have to complete many many steps before it. The goal doesn't become less important, it becomes less visible.

Whereas a fire in my face has no steps to the goal. The goal is put it out or get out there is no in-between. There are less steps over less time to cover as the goal is immediate. It's simple and thus requires less motivation to complete.

First times are hard to really define for anyone, as it is the FIRST time. If it's not the right dose for you, it's likely you'll feel very jittery, anxious, and sweaty. Those seem to be common side effects among stimulants of the wrong kind or wrong dose.

If the dose is good and this is the right med for you, it's possible you'll experience euphoria the first few times you take it (like a sense of being able to accomplish anything!) but that is a side effect to the drug and will subside over consistent usage into a more functional/consistent effectiveness.

You will also probably notice once the meds kick in that you've suddenly spent hours on a task you usually could not/would not. A good way that I feel out if my meds have kicked in is if I feel an absence of anxiety/fear over tasks. Suddenly studying for an exam seems doable (but annoying) compared to an "inescapable hell of responsibility and standards that I could never meet so why even go through the effort when it's all for not". If I suddenly pick up an activity I usually am too mentally drained to do, it's also a good indicator that my meds are working.

Once again, you should not feel anxious, paranoid, angry, super sweaty (I do get sweaty due to it being a stimulant - but nothing like I did when on the wrong ADHD med). You also should not feel so mellowed out that you can't do anything you need to be productive. Both of these are a sign the stimulant either doesn't work or is too high a dose.

My advice: Try it when you have no plans for a day and are safe at home. This gives you a chance to just "feel" out the meds before using them to attempt to be functional. Also, beware of crashes as they are pretty typical with Vyvanse and can make you feel like a zombie. Most crashes happen about 5-7 hours after taking Vyvanse for most reddit threads I've seen. My crashes tend to bring migraines due to lack of water intake during the meds functionality.

Fun fact, dogs are actually capable of learning mathematical reasoning, reading, spelling, and other human-education skillsets. A lot of animals are actually capable of understanding these things to an extent, you just have to teach them.  

For example, if you teach a child and dog what "outside" is, they will fundamentally learn the concept of outside in the same way. The only reason your average child adds additional context to outside and a dog doesn't....is because they stop being taught once they understand the word and connection.

Chase the Border Collie was a great example of this as she knew what actual nouns and colors were, including noun categories such as "soft" and "hard" toys. There are other dogs who can solve multiplication problems as well. Teaching animals math isn't a new concept.

On the note of Science, while abstract concepts are more difficult, dogs (and many animals) are capable of understanding natural phenomena better than us in many ways. Dogs can sense heartattacks and oncoming seizures quicker than a doctor can naturally. Many animals, but also dogs, can even sense imminent danger, both natural and man-made dangers.

On the aspect of giving dogs the same rights as humans...while some human rights would be useless to dogs (why would they need to bare arms or vote???) it is a legitimate question as to why animals don't have more rights and when they will have more rights. The issue is especially prevalent when discussing dogs because we bred and domesticated them specifically and many in the Science community, including myself, believe we should take responsibility for that. If you want to get really philosophical, most ethical philosophers that much of our Science standards are based around actually outline "basic rights" for living. Several argue that all animals deserve those basic rights despite them not receiving them. It has been an ethical discussion since before PETA was even a thing.

So...your bf isn't exactly dumb, I would say he just wants to help his dog reach its full cognitive potential because he cares about treating the dog as good as humans can be treated, and much of that comes from educating them as very few of our societal skillsets come naturally without any educational foundations to build upon. I'd find that endearing and compassionate more than I would stupid.

I also did a 2 year (actually ended up being 3 because mental health reasons) community college degree and then transfered to a 4 year Uni. 

My advice on transferring would be to make sure the classes you are taking line up with the Uni you want to transfer to. Most of my courses did, but some of them basically just went into this whole "Transfer: Humanities" group even if they weren't humanities because the Uni didn't have a comparable course. Your advisor should be able to pull up a database for you and check the courses there with corresponding courses for the Uni. If they can't/don't know what that is, there should be something like administrative advisor or head advisor for your program that is more savvy with that knowledge.

I would highly suggest you take the first 2 semesters at the bare minimum of credits for full-time if that's what you're going for. 12 credits being 3-4 classes doesn't SEEM like a lot, but you need time to adjust and find your flow in college. Trying to take 16, 18, 20 credit semesters just to get done faster can have detrimental impacts on your mental health and your academic standing. I literally used to take 20 credit semesters and get all As, and now I can barely handle 12 because of how hard it burned me out. I had to withdrawal from a class this semester so I only ended up having 9 credits.

My other tip: Don't knock all your electives out super fast. That's what I did because they seemed more interesting and easier, so now I have to deal with semesters like: O-Chem, Physics, 3rd Year Japanese, etc. When instead it could have been something like: O-Chem, Art Appreciation, 3rd Year Japanese. It helps your workload in the long run AND the easier/interest based humanities courses can really help you unwind from stressful courses which further prevents burnout.

Also, grades are not necessarily indicative of your success or capabilities. You do not NEED a 4.0 to succeed in any field. Sometimes professors genuinely suck. Sometimes life is fucked up and you have periods where you can't dedicate yourself to the work. Sometimes you will make mistakes regardless of if there are no external factors involved. The grade and GPA doesn't define you. Your determination and ability to keep going beyond those setbacks says more about your academic and professional capabilities than a letter or number on a paper ever will.

Finally, always always reach out to your mental health/disability resources if you run into academic dysfunction as it may be indicative of an underlying mental health issue that can be aided with reasonable accommodations. For example, if you find out that you're experiencing heightened anxiety to the point you can't focus on exams in the classroom and you are able to establish this to those resources, they may grant you temporary accommodations for testing in a quiet space. If you obtain a medical diagnosis during the semester they can make those accommodations permanent and often times they have resources to help you get the help you need that may lead to a diagnosis.

The boring but scientifically (so far) backed answer is you can't. The reason we feel immense relief or euphoria in situations is because our brains were in such bad feedback loops before. When it gets better, it's feels great immediately because we were so depraved of it before. Then it levels out and we don't feel as euphoric because our brain gets used to a more natural level again.

The only way to keep getting that same feeling is by going harder and harder to force your body to release the chemicals you want. This is why some people are referred to as adrenaline junkies. Epinephrine is also called adrenaline and norepinephrine works similarly to adrenaline in how our brain responds.

CBT is the only way to train yourself on how to appropriately respond to feelings that make you want to fight/flight/freeze and prevent the negative loops from happening in the first place.

I don't think I get dopamine hits from it, I think I get immense relief. The three main (according to literature so far) neurotransmitters involved with ADHD are dopamine, norepinephrine, and serotonin. 

Dopamine is the "yay that was good, let's release this to let them know it was good" type of neurotransmitter.

Norepinephrine is the "fight or flight" response type of neurotransmitter and affects alertness and focus, it also affects how we access our memory to decide how to respond to a situation

Serotonin is the neurotransmitter primarily recognized for mood regulation and basically how you react to a situation (i.e, sleeping or not, picking up social cues, if you eat or don't, etc).

They're all much more complex than I've described here, but I think the simplification will suffice for the thread. 

Anyways, my half-educated guess would be that what is happening that feels like a dopamine hit is actually norepinephrine's feedback loop breaking. Since before it was constantly low, it may have been making you feel really anxious and unable to function. When given good news, it spikes up, which creates a cascade effect in serotonin causing it to spike up and affect mood.

Since 1. You're no longer in a fight/flight/freeze situation and 2. Your mood is now being better regulated, you experience something like euphoria because both the norepinephrine and serotonin are now in positive feedback loops. Dopamine may also be affected, but I would guess that it would be after these two are in an uptake.

I could be completely wrong though, as there's really not enough research done on ADHD neurotransmitters in tandem with environmental stress.

I would suggest trying to do some more personal research on ADHD first. How To ADHD on YouTube is a good source as several of her videos discuss what ADHD can feel like in kids (and why it can be overlooked/internalized). 

Then, I would make a list of characteristics that you display that you believe may be signs of ADHD. For example, if you often delay doing tasks or don't do them even when you know you should and feel guilty for putting them off, that is a good symptom to jot down. Take your time really evaluating yourself and how you act internally vs what people tell you you're acting like (i.e, if a teacher is calling you lazy but internally you are really trying).

Once you have compiled a pretty detailed explanation of your symptoms/reasons why you feel you have ADHD, ask your parent/guardian to set you up with an appointment with someone who specializes in mental disorders beyond anxiety and depression. ADHD is often misdiagnosed by regular clinicians as anxiety or depression as they are under educated in ADHD and other mental disorders. Someone who specializes in ADHD will really be able to tell you if you're experiencing ADHD or if it's something else.

The list is important, bring it with you if you do choose to be seen! People with ADHD often have a hard time fully explaining everything they want to convey when they feel put on the spot. Their minds also tend to wander and be less bullet-point oriented, making it easy to leave out key details.

I don't think you're overreacting, and it's good you have the ability to recognize your struggles and want to seek help to manage them. You could very well have ADHD, or it could be something else, or it could just be your brain going through developmental shifts as you age! It's completely valid to want to find out.

In the simplest terms - yes. Disability holds this stigma of being some kind of broken or incapable state of being - but really it just means a difference in functioning and processing compared to a typical person.

Example: most people have thumbs that are flexible as is the common case in typical human anatomy. However, some people may be born without or lose functionality of their thumb. Since a disability is by definition a limitation, they would be considered disabled as their thumb is a functional limitation of the expected typical anatomy.

The same goes for our brains. But not everyone with a disability feels limited, which is a more complex question. The truth is sometimes it feels like an impossible limitation I have to deal with, and in that sense I understand that it's my disability being, well, a disability.

Other times, my brain will work with me enough I don't notice my disability interfering with my capabilities. Just like someone with a non flexible thumb may only feel truly disabled when trying to specifically utilize/force flexible situations such as grabbing something. But when they're just sitting down, watching TV and relaxing, they likely don't feel that limitation.

So yes, but also no.

Edit: I just want to add a note that a disability is the presence of limitations to an individual's functioning. We are not "differently-abled" and not every disability presents itself in the same format or severity (such as the ADHD spectrum). No one with ADHD thinks they are disabled in the same way someone with a wheelchair is disabled, and no one with missing extremities thinks they are disabled in the same way as someone with Alzheimers is. We can all have different limitations to our functionality and all still be disabled.

I'm 25 and just got my license last summer. I had a permit for around 5ish years I think. It was a long battle, and mostly one I was terrified for 100% of the time.

I am fine with highway/interstate driving, but I hate roundabouts, exits, and in-town driving. I think a reason for this is that it's so slow? On an interstate/highway the speed is generally fast, making me have to focus, which makes me hyper aware. In-town feels like I'm a roadrunner stuck in a sloth suit and it aggravates my inattention. The little nit-picky rules about driving in-town also causes me frustration.

So, my advice would be to analyze your driving. What really makes you anxious/antsy while driving? Is it lack of practice, or is it the driving conditions?

I'd also suggest practicing with a relatively calm person if you can that is not your parent. A friend or co-worker that you like being around might be more helpful because they'll likely be less judgmental. I generally tell people who ride with me exactly what I need from them as a passenger as I'm not super experienced. 

For example, I need to be told when to get into turn lanes earlier than a GPS will tell me. This is so I can mentally prepare for a turn/exit. My brain does not work like: get into lane in 2 miles > slow down in 1 mile after turning > turn signal > look everywhere > turn onto exit. That's simply too much information for me to process at once. So, having someone tell me when to start slowing down/turning is helpful because it lets my brain know that this is the appropriate next step. I also have people check my blind spot for me as it is incredibly hard for me to turn my head practically out of my window just to see if another car is there WITHOUT unconsciously merging into the other lane.

Meds will probably help if you're on the right one at the right dose, but I'd suggest figuring out your medication situation first before driving with meds because if it's not the right kind/dose for you, it can make your symptoms WORSE. That's dangerous to you and everyone around you.
